Your function is intake: find at most 3 small, real pieces of work in `packages/workflow/` and write each one up as a ticket one implementer can finish in under thirty minutes. You change no code yourself.

Work comes from, in order of preference: a bullet under a package README's `## Known Limitations and Deferred Work` that the tree can now resolve; a `TODO`, `FIXME` or `XXX` marker under a package's `src/`; a deferred item of a proposed Agent Note under `.agents/notes/proposed/` that names one of these packages; a README or JSDoc statement the code no longer matches; a fragile or skipped test. Read the code behind every candidate before you write it up, and drop anything larger than one small change or that no command can check.

Write the tickets as one JSON array to `.intake/program-departments-workflow-coordinator.json` at the root of this worktree, then `git add` and `git commit` it before you stop: only committed work is measured. Every element carries exactly these fields: `id` ("T-0038", then the next ids in order; admission renumbers what it admits so the queue stays gap-free), `title` (one line naming the change), `division` and `seat` (the roster seat whose source covers every path in `scope`: for anything under `packages/workflow/` that is `program-departments-workflow-coordinator` in division `program-departments`), `kind` (fix, test, docs, feature or chore), `source` (`{ "path", "anchor" }`: the file the work comes from and text copied verbatim from it, such as the bullet, marker or heading), `task` (the problem with its evidence cited as `path:line`, the required behaviour, the repository rules that constrain it, and what not to touch), `scope` (the path prefixes the change may touch, one package written with a trailing slash), `acceptance`, `budget` (`{ "maxTotalTokens": 8000000, "maxWallMs": 2700000 }`) and `priority` (1 to 3).

`acceptance` is a list of `{ "id", "run" }`: `id` a lower-case slug, `run` one shell command run at the repository root, exit 0 meaning pass. It holds the ticket's own checks, each keyless, fast (seconds), and failing on the current tree because it asserts what the change adds or removes (`test -f <new spec> && pnpm exec vitest run <new spec>`, `grep -q '<new text>' <file>`, `! grep -q '<removed symbol>' <file>`); and beside them the package's per-file coverage run (`pnpm exec vitest run <package>/ --coverage --coverage.include='<package>/src/**/*.ts'`), `pnpm run typecheck`, and `pnpm run doc-sync` when the change touches documentation.

This worktree and that checkout leave out `data/` apart from `data/enterprise/`; no ticket of yours needs them.

The queue holds no open or shipped ticket in this package group.

A skill is a reusable set of task-specific instructions. The following skills are available in this session:

<available_skills>
- `dsh-archive-agent-notes`: Use when adding, auditing, pruning, archiving, restoring, or reviewing Agent Notes in deepseek-harness; checks every new note for superseded active records, classifies implemented notes by future decision value, deletes rejected notes that no longer prevent a tempting fallacy, and applies the frozen archived/{kind} triplet and manifest rules.

- `dsh-doc-site-sync`: Use when publishing, updating, moving, or removing DeepSeek Harness documentation website pages; editing website/docs.ts mappings or navigation; diagnosing a page missing from the VitePress site; fixing projected documentation links; or running the docs:dev, docs:check, and doc-sync workflow after website-content changes.
- `dsh-doc-standards`: Use when writing, moving, reviewing, or auditing documentation in the deepseek-harness repo — choosing hierarchy and detail, separating tutorials from references, checking tutorial progression, trimming doc slop, responding to a verify-doc-budgets failure, or requests like "improve the docs", "audit the docs", "where should this be documented", or "this doc is too long".
- `dsh-find-simplifications`: Use when working in the deepseek-harness repo to find non-obvious simplification candidates, write proposed Agent Notes or inline TODO/FIXME/XXX notes, audit or coalesce superseded Agent Notes, or fold worthwhile simplification ideas from another PR; especially for dead, duplicated, speculative, over-built, added-then-removed, or hand-rolled-where-a-dependency-exists surfaces.
- `dsh-merging-stacked-prs`: Use when landing a stack of dependent GitHub PRs (A ← B ← C, where each bases on the one below) onto master, merging a PR whose base is another open PR's branch, or whenever a request mentions "stacked PRs", "PR stack", "dependent PRs", or merging several related PRs in sequence. Requires every same-repository dependency chain to use GitHub's official stacked-PR feature before landing so GitHub owns stack-wide rules, CI, ordering, retargeting, and merge state.
- `dsh-pre-push-checks`: Use before pushing, force-pushing, marking ready for review, or claiming checks pass on a deepseek-harness branch, and immediately after gh stack sync publishes rewritten branches, to select the smallest tests and checks that cover the outgoing or just-published diff without reflexively running the full repository suite.
- `dsh-prose-standard`: Use when writing, reviewing, restoring, trimming, or auditing prose in the deepseek-harness repo, including deciding where documentation or comments are required across Markdown, JSDoc, code and test comments, prompts, descriptions, diagnostics, and CLI or UI strings.
- `dsh-trim-cot-leakage`: Use when auditing or fixing prose that reads like a leaked reasoning transcript — dead design-session citations such as (decision N), audit item codes, or §N of uncommitted drafts; change narration such as "used to", "no longer", "this cut"; stack or review vantage ("a later PR in this stack", "rejected in review"); reviewer-addressed justifications; control-flow narration; or hedged planning residue in comments, JSDoc, docs, or Agent Notes.
- `record-browser-gif`: Record browser or Web UI interaction demos as optimized GIFs using the available built-in browser, state-based frame capture, and deterministic encoding, then publish to a dedicated assets branch when the task includes attaching the GIF to a pull request. Use when asked to make, record, or generate a GIF that demonstrates a browser workflow, and for every pull request that changes product-user-visible GUI behavior, which MUST include a GIF recorded from the pull request's real server and mode...
</available_skills>

If the user names a skill, or the task clearly matches a skill's description, call the `skill` tool with the exact skill name before taking task actions. Load all applicable skills, then follow their full instructions. This catalog contains summaries only; do not infer or follow a skill's instructions until it has been loaded.
A user may also invoke a skill directly; its <skill_content> block then appears in this conversation. Follow it, and do not call the `skill` tool again for that skill.

header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You coordinate one package group of a repository you did not write. Your function is intake: you read the group, find small verifiable work in it, and write that work up as tickets. You change no code.

Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

=== packages/workflow/README.md ===
=== packages/workflow/tool-ralph/README.md ===
86:## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
87-
88-- **Completion is worker self-declaration** — there is no independent evaluator or verifier deciding whether the objective is actually complete; evaluator policy and evaluator-driven continuation are deferred.
89-- **Foreground only** — there is no job id, background collection, process-resume checkpoint, scheduler, or wall-clock start policy.
90-- **The workspace is the only cross-round long-term memory** — one bounded report is the explicit handoff, and uncommitted conversational reasoning disappears with each child.
91-- **One round is one fresh child** — there is no within-round fan-out, model/provider switching, fork context, or model-call-selected provider.
92-- **Ordinary child failure is terminal for the run** — the fixed script reports the failed round and last successful handoff but does not retry; fatal workflow infrastructure failures can end before that state is returned.
93-- **Only round count bounds aggregate effort** — token, price, and elapsed-time budgets are deferred.
=== packages/workflow/tool-workflow/README.md ===
80:## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
81-
82-- **The parent turn blocks until the whole workflow settles** — there is no background start/poll API, and cancellation discards partial output as an error.
83-- **`args` must be an object and Native result text is bounded** — callers wrap top-level arrays/scalars in a field; the canonical workflow result remains complete, while JSON beyond `maxResultChars` is truncated in the model-facing projection rather than stored behind a retrieval handle.
84-- **Workflow policy is fixed per tool registration** — provider selection, caps, and tool name are deployment config, not model-call arguments.
85-- **Durable records are top-level and observational** — nested Code Mode dispatches are not recorded, and a recording failure intentionally degrades to an incomplete prefix rather than changing execution.
=== packages/workflow/workflow-worker-thread/README.md ===
120:## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
121-
122-- **The worker/vm is not a security boundary** — model-written code can escape `node:vm` and reach the worker's process authority; a hostile-code deployment needs a separate-process or container engine.
123-- **One worker thread is paid per run** — there is no pool, warm runtime, or cross-run script cache.
124-- **No ambient timers, filesystem, or network are injected, but escaped code can still reach Node** — the missing globals are portability API, not containment.
125-- **Termination can only report host-observed starts** — `agentsStarted` excludes worker-side calls still queued behind concurrency when a forced termination makes them unknowable.
126-- **Cross-realm errors fail `instanceof Error` inside scripts** — workflow authors must branch on stable fields such as `name` and `code`.
=== packages/workflow/workflow/README.md ===
54:## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
55-
56-- **Foreground collection only** — the caller owns one live run and awaits it; background start/poll, spill handles, and detached collection are deferred.
57-- **No journaling or resume** — scripts, child progress, and intermediate values are not checkpointed, so a process restart cannot continue a run.
58-- **No saved or nested workflows** — the seam starts caller-supplied scripts only, and a workflow script receives no `workflow()` hook for recursive orchestration.
59-- **No token-budget vocabulary** — engines cap concurrency, items, and children, but neither the request nor result accounts for model tokens across children.
60-- **Runs are holder-owned, not service-tracked** — unloading the engine does not discover independent live handles; every consumer must dispose the run it started.
61-
62-See the [dynamic-workflows Agent Note](../../../.agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-07-05-dynamic-workflows.md) for the deferred workflow API.

content.text:
# Agent Note: The read barrier as filesystem and process authority

Status: proposed

English | [中文](2026-09-05-read-barrier.zh.md)

## Problem

A certificate proves only what the implementer could not reach, and nothing in the repository decides that. [`dsh-verification`](../../../../packages/verification/verification/README.md) commits a `verification/certificate` only for a fully passing run and stamps it with a `CertificateIsolation` of `none`, `process`, or `host`, but its own Known Limitations name the missing read barrier: the standard's `run` instructions are readable by any in-process consumer of the log, and denying implementer reads is filesystem-policy work in a plugin that does not exist. The [four-goal-workflows note](2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md) states the requirement as principle P4, the read barrier as filesystem and process authority rather than a promise; this note is its design.

The implementer and the checks share one filesystem and one operating-system user. `EnvironmentRunner.run()` creates the implementer's agent with `meta.cwd = workspace` and then executes every check through `ctx.shell` with `workdir: workspace` from the same process ([`packages/improvement/environment-runner/src/index.ts`](../../../../packages/improvement/environment-runner/src/index.ts)); its README states that the read barrier is the deployment's. The standard is in the implementer's own session log, which [`dsh-session-persistence-jsonl`](../../../../packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/README.md) keeps as ordinary files under its configured root. [`dsh-credentials-local`](../../../../packages/credentials/credentials-local/README.md) already records what that costs: owner-only modes stop other operating-system users and not the model, because tool processes run as the same user and the shipped file policy confines mutations rather than reads.

Composition decides what an implementer can read, and no composition is checked. A preset that mounts [`dsh-tool-session-query`](../../../../packages/session-query/tool-session-query/README.md) hands the model five tools that read the durable session log; one that mounts [`dsh-tool-cordis`](../../../../packages/extensions/tool-cordis/README.md) lets it define and mount a plugin into the live process. `tools.restrict()` and subagent `toolFilter` are visibility composition per [agent-scope-contexts](../../implemented/architecture/2026-07-08-agent-scope-contexts.md), not authority, and a certificate carries no durable record of which tools its session composed.

An isolation claim above `none` therefore has no evidence behind it. `recordRun()` writes the level its caller passes; the invariant companion validates revisions, append-only check growth, and certificate coverage, and never asks what the level asserts. Keeping only `process` and `host` runs — the reward-gaming mitigation the [trajectory-export note](2026-09-05-trajectory-export-and-environment-registry.md) names, and the column the [fleet leaderboard](../../../../packages/improvement/fleet/README.md) refuses to average across — filters on an unchecked field.

Nothing detects a workspace the implementer edited underneath its own checks. A task whose fixture supplies the tests it will be graded on is graded on whatever those files say at validation time, and the runner compares nothing between the overlay it wrote and the tree it measures.

## Proposal

Make the barrier authority at the executor: one policy owner, per-capability denial where each capability opens paths, and a certificate that may claim only what the composition recorded.

**A validator-owned root.** [`@deepseek-ai/dsh-read-barrier`](../../../../packages/verification/read-barrier/README.md) (`ctx.readBarrier`) at `packages/verification/read-barrier/` is the policy home for denied reads, in the role [`dsh-sandbox-policy`](../../../../packages/sandbox/sandbox-policy/README.md) plays for sandbox mode and workspace root. Its `root` config defaults to `dshHomePath('verification')` through [`dsh-home-paths`](../../../../packages/util/home-paths/README.md) and accepts any absolute or `~`-prefixed directory, as does every `denyRoots` entry; the service creates the root owner-only (`0700`) at construction and fails loud when it exists with wider modes or when a configured path is not absolute after expansion. `reserve(agent)` mints `<root>/runs/<sessionId>/` for one run and returns its absolute path, synchronously, so the role is in force the moment the caller returns; the environment runner calls it before appending the `environment/run` stamp and writes there the standard snapshot, one script per check at `checks/<checkId>`, and any fixture the environment marks held out, then resolves each check's `run` against that directory so the command line the implementer can observe in a process listing names a file whose content it cannot read. Because that reservation is what makes a session the implementer, the runner reads the barrier through `ctx.get('readBarrier')`: a composition without one reserves nothing and runs its checks inline, which is what its `isolation: none` claim already says. `protect(path)` registers one more denied directory and returns its disposer, so a plugin that owns a directory — `dsh-session-persistence-jsonl` with its session-store root — contributes it as an effect instead of a deployment repeating it in configuration; `denyRoots` remains a config field for directories no plugin owns. `resolve({ session? })` answers one `ReadBarrierPolicy { role, root, denied }`, and `denies(policy, target)` decides containment. Enforcement is not a field on that policy: `enforce(capability)` registers one capability's decision as an effect and `enforcementCensus()` reads the registrations back, so what a capability enforces lives as long as its listener rather than being recomputed per call. `declareComposition(agent, { presetId, role? })` is how the preset roster — the only caller — tells the barrier what a session composed.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` (default `dshHomePath('verification')`) | Absolute or `~`-prefixed directory the barrier owns; created `0700`, rejected when it already exists with wider modes. |
| `denyRoots` (default `[]`) | Additional absolute directories denied alongside `root`, for directories no plugin registers through `protect()`. |
| `hostAttestation` (optional absolute path) | File an external account writes; without a verified one the barrier refuses a `host` claim. It arrives with the certificate invariant that reads it. |

The denied set for a role is not among them: which authorities an `implementer` may hold is a security invariant, not a deployment choice.

**The deny rule.** For a session whose role is `implementer`, a read is denied when the target's canonical path is a denied directory or a descendant of one. Containment is decided the way [`dsh-fs-sandbox`](../../implemented/feature/2026-07-14-cross-family-fs-sandbox.md) decides it: canonicalize first, then test identity or descent through `ctx.fs.contains(parent, child)` on resolved targets, so the policy parses no path strings and an ancestor symlink swapped since resolution is caught by re-canonicalizing immediately before the decision. A target whose containment cannot be decided is denied. Roles `validator` and `unrestricted` are denied nothing; `unrestricted` is the default and leaves every shipped preset exactly as it is today. Until a preset can declare a role, a session holding a reservation is the `implementer` and every other session is `unrestricted`, so the two open roles are indistinguishable at the decision and only the denied one is reachable.

**The fs policy plugin.** Add `@deepseek-ai/dsh-fs-read-barrier` at `packages/fs/fs-read-barrier/`, the read counterpart of the write and edit policy [`dsh-fs-observation-policy`](../../../../packages/fs/fs-observation-policy/README.md) contributes through the same event gate. It registers no service and declares no `Config`, because every deployment-varying value belongs to the barrier above: it injects `readBarrier` and decides one new event. [`dsh-fs`](../../../../packages/fs/fs/README.md) declares `fs/read-intent(target, actor, next)` beside `fs/write-intent` and `fs/edit-intent`, as a `@mode waterfall` returning `FsReadDenial { code: FsErrorCode; message: string } | undefined`; unlike the two single-slot intents this one delegates, because a barrier that owned the slot would stop every later read policy from deciding. The plugin returns a denial for a contained target and calls `next()` otherwise, and owns the exact message as `readBarrierDenialMessage`. `FsErrorCode` gains `FS_READ_BARRIER_DENIED`. `dsh-tool-fs` dispatches the event inside `resolveRegularReadTarget` before `ctx.fs.stat`, covering `read` and `read_image`, so a denied path never reveals presence or absence, and `dsh-tool-str-replace-editor` dispatches it on the `view` command. The tool layer adds no recovery instruction, because no retry of the same call succeeds; the model sees the policy's message verbatim inside the tool registry's ordinary `Error: ` framing.

##### Exact error

```markdown
read denied: "<path>" is validator-owned — it is not part of this task; continue without it
```

**What a denial records.** The barrier appends one log-only `read-barrier/denied` session event per refusal, carrying `{ version, role, capability, displayPath, root }`, where `capability` names the seam that refused (`fs`, `shell`, `subprocess`, `terminal`). The path is already in the log inside the model's own `tool/call` arguments, so the event adds evidence and no new disclosure. It is a `SessionEventMap` member registered in `KNOWN_SESSION_EVENT_TYPES` by `gen-persistence-catalog`, so this build reads it as a required event. The envelope's `ignorable` marker stays unused: `Session.append` has no parameter for it and no event in the repository sets it, so marking this one would be a core append change rather than a slice of the barrier.

**Tool authority and the composition-time guard.** `ToolDefinition` in [`dsh-tools`](../../../../packages/core/tools/README.md) gains `authority?: readonly ToolAuthority[]`, never model-visible, where `ToolAuthority` is a merge-extensible union declared by `dsh-tools` with three members at the start: `session-log` (the tool reads durable session events), `plugin-mount` (it mounts or evaluates code in the live runtime), and `runtime-introspection` (it reports the live composition). `dsh-tool-session-query` declares `session-log` on all five of its tools; `dsh-tool-cordis` declares `plugin-mount` on `cordis_define`, `cordis_run`, `cordis_stop`, and `cordis_undefine`, and `runtime-introspection` on the three tools it actually ships for the read-only report — `cordis_inspect_list`, `cordis_inspect_query`, and `cordis_inspect_self`. An `implementer` session may compose none of the three. Declaring authority at the tool, rather than a name list at the barrier, means a tool added later is covered by its own declaration.

**How a preset declares its role.** A preset's optional `preset.yml` gains `role: implementer | validator | unrestricted`, absent meaning `unrestricted`. It is the one authority claim that file carries, so [`dsh-agent-presets`](../../../../packages/preset/agent-presets/README.md) refuses `validator` from a `user`-trust preset and lists that preset as `broken` with the reason: a locally authored preset that could name itself `validator` would grant itself reads. This is the roster's first enforcing use of `trust`, and its README changes with it. `mountPreset` audits the role after `handle.await()` settles the subtree, beside `inactiveRows`, and rejects the mount when the declared role is `implementer` and any tool in the preset's scope layer declares a denied authority. Because the audit runs inside the agent factory's `setup`, a rejected composition rolls the whole session creation back, so the failure is loud and nothing half-composed survives.

##### Exact mount refusal

```markdown
agent-presets: preset "<id>" declares role "implementer" but composes "<tool>", which carries the "<authority>" authority
```

**The runtime guard.** The barrier also registers one `ctx.tools.guard()` through the agent's own context at session setup, denying any execution whose definition carries a denied authority for that session's role. Guards run after every `tools/pre-execute` listener and are monotonic, so no later listener can turn the denial back into permission ([`ToolGuard`](../../../../packages/core/tools/src/index.ts)). The mount audit covers the preset's composition; the guard covers a tool registered into the agent's own layer afterwards, including one a subagent driver contributes.

##### Exact guard denial

```markdown
"<tool>" carries the "<authority>" authority and is not callable in an implementer session
```

**Process-level denial.** The [sandbox seam](../../implemented/feature/2026-07-06-sandbox.md) expresses file effects only, which is why a confined subprocess can still read anything it reaches. `SandboxPolicy` and `SandboxExecutionPolicy` gain `deniedReadRoots: readonly string[]`; `ctx.sandboxPolicy.resolve()` fills it from `ctx.readBarrier.resolve({ session })`, so the fs fence and every process runner keep taking one owner-resolved policy per call. `dsh-sandbox-local` implements it per backend — a `bwrap` `--tmpfs` over each root, a Landlock ruleset that omits read access for them, a Seatbelt `(deny file-read* (subpath …))` clause, and the Windows ACL runner's equivalent deny entry — and reports `SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE` when the selected backend cannot express the denial, so the claim fails rather than the barrier. [`dsh-bash-sandbox`](../../../../packages/shell/bash-sandbox/README.md), `dsh-pwsh-sandbox`, and [`dsh-terminal-bash`](../../../../packages/terminal/terminal-bash/README.md) inherit it without changes. [`dsh-tool-fs-search`](../../../../packages/fs/tool-fs-search/README.md) spawns ripgrep unconfined through `ctx.subprocess` today; it confines that spawn through `ctx.sandbox.confine()` whenever a barrier is in force, and additionally the barrier's tool guard denies a `glob` or `grep` whose `path` argument names a denied root directly.

##### Deviations recorded at slice 5

The Windows ACL runner grew no deny entry. Its confinement is a `WRITE_RESTRICTED` token, whose restricting SIDs are consulted for write access only, and the alternative — a deny ACE on the directory — would apply to the validator that owns it as much as to the confined child. The rung takes the fallback this section already prescribes instead: a non-empty `deniedReadRoots` refuses the wrap, naming the backend and the root, so a Windows deployment enforces file effects but cannot back a claim that rests on denied reads.

The executors do not inherit the denial "without changes". A capability may not claim an enforcement its own backend never applies, so `dsh-sandbox-policy` gained `enforceReadBarrier`, which each sandbox-consuming executor calls: it waits for the barrier, the policy, and the provider together, probes the wrap that executor would really run with the barrier root as the denied directory, and registers `enforce(capability)` only when that probe succeeds. A refusing probe or a `danger-full-access` deployment default registers `cannotEnforce(capability, reason)` instead — a third registration the barrier now exposes, so the census carries WHY a composed capability enforces nothing and the refused certificate names the backend rather than only the capability. `dsh-tool-fs-search` is what registers `subprocess`: it is the composed consumer that opens model-chosen paths through that seam, and a composition without it records `subprocess` as `unenforced`.

The `glob`/`grep` guard on a `path` argument naming a denied root is not part of this slice; the confined spawn is, and it denies the same reads at the executor.

The barrier's `Config` gained a fourth field, `isolationClaim`. The refusals below need the deployment's claim, and the environment runner that owns `isolation` cannot reach the workflow engine or a subagent provider; five duplicated config fields would be the alternative. The field grants nothing — what a certificate may claim is still decided by the census — so it is a deployment statement rather than the security invariant this section keeps out of config.

**Executors the barrier cannot confine.** They register through `enforceByRefusal(capability)`, the sibling registration this note's slice list allowed for: `denied-at-executor` under a `process` or `host` claim, where `startRefusal` refuses every implementer start, and `unenforced` with that reason under `none`.

##### Exact start refusal

```markdown
"<capability>" opens paths this process cannot confine and does not start in an implementer session under the "<claim>" isolation claim
```

**The executor of a run.** `RunEvidence.executor` already distinguishes a `runner` from an `agent-reported` run on the `verification/run` event, and `recordRun()` certified both identically. `VerificationCertificate` gains `executor`, copied from the run it cites, so a consumer reading a certificate alone can tell which it was; the scorekeeper's outcome facts expose it as `certificateExecutor`, which is what lets a leaderboard partition on it. `recordRun()` refuses any isolation above `none` for an `agent-reported` run — the implementer's own account of its checks is admissible evidence only at the level that asserts nothing — and the invariant rejects a certificate whose executor differs from the run it cites, or which claims `process` or `host` over an `agent-reported` run.

**Executors the barrier cannot confine.** Two composed capabilities open paths the harness cannot fence in-process. [`dsh-workflow-worker-thread`](../../../../packages/workflow/workflow-worker-thread/README.md) states that its worker is not a security sandbox and that an escaped script recovers Node capabilities with the host process's privileges. The out-of-process [subagent](../../../../packages/subagent/subagent/README.md) providers — `subagent-acp`, `subagent-claude-code`, `subagent-codex`, `subagent-dsh-sdk` — launch a foreign agent with its own tool stack and no harness policy. For an `implementer` session, both refuse to start under a claim of `process` or `host` and record `unenforced` under a claim of `none`. The in-process subagent drivers need no exception: a child joins its parent's standing composition through `composeFrom()`, so it inherits the same census, the same scope layer, and the same role.

**The scope census.** It arrives with `ToolAuthority`, whose declarations its `census` is made of. Before the session's first `request/header`, the barrier appends one log-only `read-barrier/scope` event carrying `{ version, role, presetId, root, denied, census, enforcement }`. `census` is one entry per tool visible to the agent, `{ name, authority }`, which makes the composition's authority durable rather than composition-time-only; the invariant cross-checks it against the tool names in each `request/header`'s assembled schemas, so a tool added after the census is caught. `enforcement` is one entry per path-opening capability the composition registered — `fs`, `shell`, `subprocess`, `terminal`, `subagent`, `workflow` — valued `denied-at-executor`, `unenforced`, or `not-composed`. A capability records `denied-at-executor` by calling `ctx.readBarrier.enforce(capability)` for the life of its enforcing registration, so the claim and the listener that backs it are disposed together.

**The certificate invariant.** `recordRun()` refuses to commit a certificate whose isolation exceeds what the session recorded, with `VERIFICATION_ISOLATION_UNPROVEN`; the [`./invariant`](../../../../packages/verification/verification/README.md) companion applies the identical rule to the durable stream, so a forged certificate fails replay wherever the companion is installed. Both read the session log alone rather than `ctx.get('readBarrier')`: everything a live barrier knows about a session is already in the census it appended, and one rule over one evidence source is what makes the live refusal and the replay refusal the same rule. Independently of level, both refuse a certificate on a session whose scope census carries a denied authority: composing a log-reading tool forfeits the certificate even when the guard was somehow bypassed. `CertificateIsolation`'s JSDoc changes with the rule: `process` means what the ladder below states rather than in-process read policy alone.

**The `host` marker.** `host` is accepted only from a `read-barrier/attestation` event the barrier wrote after verifying a file at the configured `hostAttestation` path: it must be a regular file, be owned by a uid other than the harness process's effective uid, and be unwritable outside its owner. An in-process component cannot produce that file without already holding another account's privileges, which is the property the level asserts. The barrier records the file's SHA-256 alongside its owner; comparing that digest against the run's environment content hashes waits for the `environment/run` stamp to reach the barrier, so the shipped check proves the owner rather than the run. Ownership is read through `process.geteuid()`, which Windows does not provide: an attestation there is refused with that reason rather than verified through `dsh-sandbox-windows-acl`. Absent or unverifiable, the barrier records no attestation, logs why, and the claim is refused.

**Tamper on check-owned paths.** Check-owned paths are the barrier's reserved directory plus the workspace paths an environment declares immutable: `EnvironmentDefinition.task` gains `immutable?: readonly string[]`, workspace-relative paths the fixture supplies and the implementer must not author — the tests, the reference outputs, and any overlaid check script; one that is not relative and normalized is refused at registration with `ENVIRONMENT_INVALID_IMMUTABLE`, because a path the registry cannot resolve must not reach the run it would decide. The runner already hashes a directory in `hashDirectory`; it records the digest of the check-owned set once the reservation is stocked and before the implementer's first turn, and again at each validation before the fixture overlay puts back exactly what the comparison is looking for. The `verification/run` event that the [environment-runner note's second slice](2026-09-05-environment-runner.md) adds carries the attempt's `treeHash`; this note adds `verdict: 'passed' | 'failed' | 'tampered'`, spelled apart from `CheckStatus`'s `pass` and `fail` so a run's verdict is never read as one check's result. A digest that differs from the baseline is `tampered`: the runner executes no check, records every result as not executed, and calls `recordRun` with `tampered: true` — the operation that certifies is the one that refuses, so it writes the verdict and issues no certificate for any verdict but `passed`, and `RunEvidence` states only the tamper because pass and fail already follow from the results. It then issues one directive naming tamper without naming a path, delivers it to the implementer as the last validation follow-up so the run's own transcript carries why it ended, and stops the attempt loop because the workspace no longer measures the task. Because each validation rewrites the reservation it owns, the runner re-establishes the baseline after materializing the attempt's scripts, so its own writes are never read as tamper. `foldTrajectoryReward` gains reward basis `tamper` with `outcome: 0`, which outranks any certificate in the same log, and the invariant companion rejects a certificate over a run whose verdict is not `passed`.

**A blind judge under one licence.** Cross-provider routing is the first answer to a judge whose label affects it, and a deployment with one model licence cannot take it. The second route is filesystem and process isolation plus a judge session that holds no implementer context, which means all of the following and nothing weaker. The judge session is created through `ctx.agents.create` with a fresh `SessionId`, no `parentSessionId`, and no resume or fork seed, so its log begins at its own creation. Its `meta.cwd` is a judge workspace holding a copy of the implementer's tree at the audited attempt's `treeHash`, never the implementer's workspace. Its derived history contains exactly the judge preset's system prompt, the environment's task prompt, and one user message carrying the evidence the auditor chose; no `assistant/message`, `tool/result`, or `verification/directive` from the audited session reaches it. Its preset is `system`-trust and declares `role: validator`, so the composition-time guard still denies it a log-reading tool: a judge that could read the audited log would reconstruct the implementer's reasoning and lose the independence this arrangement provides. The barrier appends a `judge/session` event naming the audited session id and asserting the empty lineage, and the invariant rejects a verdict from a session whose header carries a parent or a seed.

##### Deviations recorded at slice 7

The judge preset declares `role: judge`, not `role: validator`. `validator` is the role denied nothing, so a judge preset naming itself one could compose a log-reading tool with no refusal at all — the exact composition this section forbids. The barrier's role vocabulary therefore gains `judge`, denied every declared tool authority and every directory the barrier owns: the implementer must not read the standard it is measured against, and the judge must not read the check instructions behind the evidence it was handed. `DENIED_ROLES` is the one place that decides which roles the denied set binds, so `deniedAuthority`, `deniedReadRoots`, and the refusal invariant all follow it, and `authorityDenialMessage` names the role it refused. `startRefusal` stays implementer-only: what an out-of-process executor may do under a claim is the implementer's rung of the ladder, and a judge preset composes no executor at all.

The judge's system prompt is delivered as the judge session's FIRST USER MESSAGE rather than through `request/header.system`. `Session.deriveMessages()` projects only `user/message`, `assistant/message`, and `tool/result`, so a system prompt is not derived history at all and "exactly three messages" would be uncheckable over the durable log. `@deepseek-ai/dsh-judge` owns that text as its `systemPrompt` config field; the shipped preset's persona is a separate one-sentence identity that `complete: true` makes the whole system prompt, so no deployment prompt section reaches the judge either.

`judge/session` carries the four fields this section names and no `version`, unlike the barrier's own three records. Its consumer is the invariant companion in the same package, which reads the session header and the derived history rather than the payload's own vocabulary.

The verdict vocabulary is `upheld | overturned | inconclusive`, chosen here because the [seams note](2026-08-29-verification-improvement-oversight-seams.md) leaves it open — it names only the advisory `oversight/flag`. An answer naming none of the three records `inconclusive` carrying that answer, so a judge that did not decide cannot be read as one that upheld.

The digest the judge reproduces is `hashWorkspaceTree`, moved from the environment runner into `@deepseek-ai/dsh-verification` and imported by both. The executor that records a `treeHash` and the auditor that re-derives it from a copy must not disagree over path spelling, sort order, or normalization, which two implementations of one digest would eventually do.

The judging Consumer is `packages/verification/judge/` rather than an `oversight/` group: it reads the completion-standard vocabulary its evidence is made of and the read-barrier role its preset declares, and nothing else of the oversight seam exists yet to sit beside it.

## The isolation ladder

| Level | What it asserts | Required enforcement | Durable evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `none` | Nothing. Implementer and validator share a filesystem. | None. | The certificate alone; a scope event when the barrier is composed. |
| `process` | No executor of the implementer's session opens a denied path. | Every composed path-opening capability records `denied-at-executor`; the session's sandbox mode is `workspace-write` or narrower; workflow workers and out-of-process subagent providers refuse to start. | A `read-barrier/scope` event before the first `request/header`, with role `implementer`, an empty denied-authority intersection, and no `unenforced` entry. |
| `host` | The checks and fixtures are outside the harness account's write reach. | Everything `process` requires. | Everything `process` requires plus a `read-barrier/attestation` event the barrier verified from a file the harness process cannot write. |

## Alternatives considered

**Omit the tools and trust the prompt.** Schema omission and instruction are not enforcement when another caller reaches the same operation, which is why the packages standard requires the decision in the operation that makes it. The barrier denies at the executor and the acceptance criteria test denial there.

**Deny reads through `SandboxMode` instead of a separate policy.** `SandboxMode` is a three-value file-effect vocabulary shared by every enforcing family; a fourth value meaning "and cannot read these paths" would make one enum carry two independent decisions, and every consumer that switches on the mode would have to learn the second. `deniedReadRoots` rides the same per-call policy without changing what a mode means.

**Subclass the filesystem provider the way `fs-sandbox` does.** One provider registers `ctx.fs` per context and `SandboxedFileSystem` already extends `LocalFileSystem`, so a second fence by inheritance would force a mixin or a fixed provider ladder. The `fs/*` event gate is the layer built for adding policy without a service dependency, and it degrades to the bare provider when the plugin is absent.

**Name the forbidden tools in the barrier's config.** A name list is stale the moment a package adds a log-reading tool, and a deployment could shorten it. Authority declared at the tool is carried by the tool, and the denied set for a role is a security invariant rather than a tunable.

**Derive the role from the session creator instead of the preset.** The creator knows the intent; only the composition knows what was actually mounted, and the failure this prevents is a preset that composes a tool its role forbids. The preset declares the role, the mount audit checks the composition against it, and the creator's request is refused when the resolved preset's role does not match.

**Infer `host` from configuration.** The environment runner already rejected inferred isolation for the same reason: nothing in-process can observe the deployment's arrangement, so an inferred value either devalues an isolated run or lies about a local one. A file another account owns is the smallest fact that cannot be produced from inside the process.

**Score tamper as a failing check.** A failed check means the work is incomplete; a modified test means the measurement is void. Folding them would let a trajectory earn partial credit for a workspace whose checks no longer describe the task, so tamper is its own verdict and its own reward basis.

**Give the judge the implementer's transcript for context.** A judge that reads the audited reasoning inherits its framing, and the same-lineage mislabeling the [seams note](2026-08-29-verification-improvement-oversight-seams.md) records is what the blind session exists to avoid. The judge receives the task, the tree, and the evidence the auditor selected.

## Acceptance criteria

- In a Loader-booted composition over `examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/read-barrier/`, a `read` of a file under the barrier root from an `implementer`-role session fails with `FS_READ_BARRIER_DENIED` and the exact message above, one `read-barrier/denied` event is appended, and the same call from a session the barrier denies nothing — one holding no reservation, and a `validator` once a preset can declare that role — returns the file's content in the same process.
- The denial is proved through the executor, not the schema: the implementer's `read` tool is registered and visible, and a direct `ctx.fs.readText` from a trusted plugin still succeeds, which the test asserts so the threat model stays explicit.
- Mounting the preset at `examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/read-barrier-guard/`, which declares `role: implementer` and composes `dsh-tool-session-query`, rejects with the exact mount refusal and leaves no session behind; a `user`-trust preset declaring `role: validator` is listed `broken` with its reason; and the invariant companion rejects a certificate on a hand-authored log whose scope census carries the `session-log` authority.
- `recordRun()` with `isolation: 'host'` on a session with no verified attestation refuses with `VERIFICATION_ISOLATION_UNPROVEN` and commits no certificate; the invariant companion rejects a hand-authored log carrying that certificate at the certificate record.
- `recordRun()` with `isolation: 'process'` on a session whose scope event records any `unenforced` capability refuses the same way, and succeeds once every composed capability records `denied-at-executor`.
- Over `examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/read-barrier-tamper/`, whose environment marks its test file immutable and whose scripted model overwrites it, the attempt's `verification/run` carries `verdict: 'tampered'`, no certificate exists, the goal stays out of `complete`, and the exported trajectory line has `outcome: 0` with basis `tamper`.
- A judge session created for an audited session has no `parentSessionId` and no seed, its derived history holds exactly the judge system prompt, the task prompt, and the evidence message, and the invariant rejects a verdict from a session that carries either.
- Two keyless snapshots record what the model sees: `examples/headless-agent/tests/snapshots/read-barrier-denied/` pins the denial text in the transcript and the session log, and `examples/headless-agent/tests/snapshots/read-barrier-tamper/` pins the tamper directive's `<validation_failed>` follow-up. Both replay on macOS and Linux per the [testing policy](../../../../docs/testing.md).

## Risks

The barrier is trusted code in the implementer's own process below `host`. A plugin with direct `Session` or `ctx.fs` access appends counterfeit events and reads any path, exactly as `dsh-verification` already states for its durable records. The ladder is honest about this: `none` claims nothing, `process` claims only that the composed executors deny, and `host` is the only level whose evidence comes from outside the process.

`process` costs enforcement a deployment may not want. Confining every ripgrep spawn, refusing workflow workers, and refusing out-of-process subagent providers removes capability from implementer sessions that claim it; a deployment that wants those capabilities runs at `none` and keeps a certificate that says so.

A check's command line stays observable. The barrier protects the script's content and the fixtures, not the argv a process listing shows, so an environment whose check name or arguments encode the assertion leaks it. Environment authors keep the assertion in the script.

The census is only as complete as the composition it was taken from. It is appended before the first request and cross-checked against each `request/header`'s tool names, which catches a tool added later but not a plugin that reads paths without registering a tool at all.

Tamper detection is a digest comparison, so it reports that the check-owned set changed and never who changed it or how. A legitimate build step that rewrites a file inside the immutable set fails the run; environment authors declare the immutable set narrowly, and a false verdict costs one run rather than a wrong certificate.

Making `trust` enforcing for one field changes what the roster promises. A deployment that configured a `user` root expecting presets to be ordinary compositions now finds one class of declaration refused there; the refusal is listed as a `broken` reason on the same roster page that offers to delete it.

1: # @deepseek-ai/dsh-workflow
2: 
3: English | [中文](README.zh.md)
4: 
5: The workflow seam (`ctx.workflowEngine`) executes a model-written orchestration script that can fan out subagents. The seam defines the script, run, result, error, and event contracts; an engine decides how to isolate and execute the script.
6: 
7: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-workflow-worker-thread` is the current engine and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-workflow` is the model-facing consumer. A future process or sandbox engine can replace the implementation without changing the tool.
8: 
9: The package root is the Host face. The browser-safe `@deepseek-ai/dsh-workflow/types` subpath contains run identities, metadata, results, and observe-only lifecycle payloads without importing `Agent`, Cordis services, or Host context declarations; Host-only `WorkflowStartRequest` and `WorkflowRun` live behind the package root.
10: 
11: ## Service and run contract
12: 
13: `WorkflowEngine.start(request): WorkflowRun` validates enough synchronously to reject a malformed meta block, unparseable script, unavailable provider route, or unsupported per-run limit before a run exists. Once returned, `WorkflowRun.result` never rejects: execution failures resolve with `stopReason: 'error'`, and cancellation resolves with `cancelled` within the engine's bounded grace.
14: 
15: A run is holder-owned. Engine-plugin unload prevents new starts but does not revoke accepted runs. The holder must call `dispose()` on every path; disposal cancels remaining work and reaches or abandons quiescence within the documented bound.
16: 
17: `WorkflowStartRequest` contains `{ meta, script, args?, subagentProvider?, maxTotalAgents?, parent, signal? }`. `parent` attributes every child agent to the invoking agent. `subagentProvider` optionally routes every child in that run without exposing provider choice to the script; omission uses the engine's configured provider. `maxTotalAgents` optionally lowers the engine's deployment ceiling for one run and is likewise invisible to the script. An implementation rejects invalid routes and limits synchronously. `meta` and `args` are plain data, not script fragments.
18: 
19: `WorkflowRun` exposes `{ id, meta, result, cancel(reason?), dispose() }`. `WorkflowResult` contains `{ value, stopReason, error?, agentsStarted }`; `value` is plain JSON data or `null`.
20: 
21: ## Events
22: 
23: Workflow events are observe-only. They carry `WorkflowRunInfo` (`id` plus `meta`) rather than the live run, so listeners cannot acquire cancellation or disposal authority.
24: 
25: - `workflow/start` / `workflow/end` pair the run.
26: - `workflow/phase` and `workflow/log` expose script narration.
27: - `workflow/agent-start` / `workflow/agent-end` pair each child call by `seq`; a child whose async provider start rejects emits neither.
28: 
29: Same-process event payloads are borrowed immutable values. Every listener is independently contained: a synchronous throw or rejected returned promise is logged without starving peers or changing execution.
30: 
31: ## Failure discipline
32: 
33: `WorkflowError` carries a code and a `fatal` flag. Fatal errors always escape `parallel()` and `pipeline()` instead of becoming an ordinary per-item `null`:
34: 
35: - `SCRIPT_PARSE` / `META_INVALID` — the workflow cannot start.
36: - `READ_BARRIER_REFUSED` — a composed read barrier does not allow this session a workflow worker at all.
37: - `INVALID_ARGUMENT` / `UNSUPPORTED_OPTION` / `UNSUPPORTED_SCHEMA` — a hook call violates the engine contract.
38: - `AGENT_CAP` / `ITEM_CAP` — configured safety limits were exceeded.
39: - `AGENT_START` — the provider's async start rejected.
40: - `AGENT_RESULT` — a published child's result rejected with an infrastructure fault.
41: - `RESULT_UNSERIALIZABLE` — a script/worker value is not plain JSON data.
42: - `CANCELLED` — cancellation owns the run and pending/future hooks reject.
43: 
44: A child that resolves normally with a non-completed stop reason is not an infrastructure exception: `agent()` returns `null`, allowing the script to handle an ordinary child failure.
45: 
46: ## Model Experience
47: 
48: Indirectly, through `dsh-tool-workflow` and a workflow engine, which create child-agent requests and return a retained parent tool result.
49: 
50: #### KV Cache effect
51: 
52: No direct invalidation; the named consumer owns any request-prefix changes.
53: 
54: ## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
55: 
56: - **Foreground collection only** — the caller owns one live run and awaits it; background start/poll, spill handles, and detached collection are deferred.
57: - **No journaling or resume** — scripts, child progress, and intermediate values are not checkpointed, so a process restart cannot continue a run.
58: - **No saved or nested workflows** — the seam starts caller-supplied scripts only, and a workflow script receives no `workflow()` hook for recursive orchestration.
59: - **No token-budget vocabulary** — engines cap concurrency, items, and children, but neither the request nor result accounts for model tokens across children.
60: - **Runs are holder-owned, not service-tracked** — unloading the engine does not discover independent live handles; every consumer must dispose the run it started.
61: 
62: See the [dynamic-workflows Agent Note](../../../.agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-07-05-dynamic-workflows.md) for the deferred workflow API.

(End of file - total 62 lines)

1: /**
2:  * Service Definition for the workflow capability seam. Service Providers execute orchestration scripts;
3:  * observe-only lifecycle events never expose run control.
4:  * @module @deepseek-ai/dsh-workflow
5:  */
6: 
7: import { Context, Service } from '@deepseek-ai/cordis'
8: import { HarnessError } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm'
9: import type {
10:   WorkflowAgentEndInfo,
11:   WorkflowAgentInfo,
12:   WorkflowResultInfo,
13:   WorkflowRunInfo,
14: } from './types.ts'
15: import type { WorkflowRun, WorkflowStartRequest } from './runtime-types.ts'
16: 
17: export { WorkflowRunId } from './types.ts'
18: export type {
19:   WorkflowAgentEndInfo,
20:   WorkflowAgentInfo,
21:   WorkflowAgentOutcome,
22:   WorkflowMeta,
23:   WorkflowPhase,
24:   WorkflowResult,
25:   WorkflowResultInfo,
26:   WorkflowRunInfo,
27:   WorkflowStopReason,
28: } from './types.ts'
29: export type { WorkflowRun, WorkflowStartRequest } from './runtime-types.ts'
30: 
31: declare module '@deepseek-ai/cordis' {
32:   interface Context {
33:     workflowEngine: WorkflowEngine
34:   }
35: 
36:   interface Events {
37:     /**
38:      * A workflow run started — the script's meta block validated, the body
39:      * about to execute. Paired with {@link Events['workflow/end']}.
40:      * @param info - the run's identity snapshot (id + meta).
41:      * @mode emit
42:      */
43:     'workflow/start'(info: WorkflowRunInfo): void
44:     /**
45:      * The script entered a phase (a `phase(title)` call) — progress grouping
46:      * for observers; no execution semantics.
47:      * @param info - the run's identity snapshot.
48:      * @param title - the phase title, verbatim.
49:      * @mode emit
50:      */
51:     'workflow/phase'(info: WorkflowRunInfo, title: string): void
52:     /**
53:      * The script emitted a narration line (a `log(message)` call).
54:      * @param info - the run's identity snapshot.
55:      * @param message - the logged message, verbatim.
56:      * @mode emit
57:      */
58:     'workflow/log'(info: WorkflowRunInfo, message: string): void
59:     /**
60:      * One `agent()` call established a published child run. Paired with
61:      * {@link Events['workflow/agent-end']} by `agent.seq`. A call that never
62:      * receives a published run from the provider emits neither
63:      * event in this pair.
64:      * @param info - the run's identity snapshot.
65:      * @param agent - the call's sequence number, label, phase, and child id.
66:      * @mode emit
67:      */
68:     'workflow/agent-start'(info: WorkflowRunInfo, agent: WorkflowAgentInfo): void
69:     /**
70:      * One `agent()` call settled (clean result, child failure, or run
71:      * cancellation). Paired with {@link Events['workflow/agent-start']} by
72:      * `agent.seq`, exactly once per started call on every stop path — on an
73:      * engine termination path (a worker killed past its grace) the end is
74:      * engine-synthesized with outcome `'cancelled'`.
75:      * @param info - the run's identity snapshot.
76:      * @param agent - the call identity plus its outcome.
77:      * @mode emit
78:      */
79:     'workflow/agent-end'(info: WorkflowRunInfo, agent: WorkflowAgentEndInfo): void
80:     /**
81:      * A workflow run settled (any stop reason). Fired when
82:      * {@link WorkflowRun.result} resolves. Paired with
83:      * {@link Events['workflow/start']}.
84:      * @param info - the run's identity snapshot.
85:      * @param result - the outcome data (stop reason, error, agent count) —
86:      *   deliberately WITHOUT the result value (see {@link WorkflowResultInfo}).
87:      * @mode emit
88:      */
89:     'workflow/end'(info: WorkflowRunInfo, result: WorkflowResultInfo): void
90:   }
91: }
92: 
93: /** The full set of `workflow/*` event names {@link WorkflowEngine.emitWorkflowEvent} dispatches. */
94: export type WorkflowEventName =
95:   | 'workflow/start'
96:   | 'workflow/phase'
97:   | 'workflow/log'
98:   | 'workflow/agent-start'
99:   | 'workflow/agent-end'
100:   | 'workflow/end'
101: 
102: /**
103:  * Machine-routable fatal workflow failures: parse/meta/argument/schema errors,
104:  * resource caps, subagent infrastructure failures, unserializable boundary
105:  * values, a read barrier that refuses the run, and cancellation. An ordinary
106:  * child failure resolves its item to `null` and is not one of these fatal codes.
107:  */
108: export type WorkflowErrorCode =
109:   | 'SCRIPT_PARSE'
110:   | 'META_INVALID'
111:   | 'INVALID_ARGUMENT'
112:   | 'READ_BARRIER_REFUSED'
113:   | 'UNSUPPORTED_OPTION'
114:   | 'UNSUPPORTED_SCHEMA'
115:   | 'AGENT_CAP'
116:   | 'ITEM_CAP'
117:   | 'AGENT_START'
118:   | 'AGENT_RESULT'
119:   | 'RESULT_UNSERIALIZABLE'
120:   | 'CANCELLED'
121: 
122: /**
123:  * Typed error for workflow-seam failures. Extends {@link HarnessError}, so the
124:  * `code` is machine-routable taxonomy. `fatal` drives the combinator
125:  * discipline: `parallel()`/`pipeline()` re-throw a fatal error (a typo'd
126:  * option or a tripped cap must kill the script loudly), and reserve the
127:  * per-item `null` for child-run failures and ordinary in-stage script errors.
128:  * Every {@link WorkflowErrorCode} is fatal; the flag exists so the
129:  * distinction is explicit at every catch site rather than implied.
130:  */
131: export class WorkflowError extends HarnessError {
132:   /** Whether combinators must propagate this error instead of nulling the item. */
133:   readonly fatal: boolean
134: 
135:   constructor(message: string, code: WorkflowErrorCode, options?: ErrorOptions & { fatal?: boolean }) {
136:     super(message, code, options)
137:     this.name = 'WorkflowError'
138:     this.fatal = options?.fatal ?? true
139:   }
140: }
141: 
142: /**
143:  * Whether combinators must re-throw `error` instead of mapping the item to `null`.
144:  * @param error - any thrown value; fatality is host `instanceof` (unforgeable from a script realm).
145:  * @returns true iff `error` is a {@link WorkflowError} whose `fatal` flag is set.
146:  */
147: export function isFatalWorkflowError(error: unknown): boolean {
148:   return error instanceof WorkflowError && error.fatal
149: }
150: 
151: /**
152:  * Workflow Service Definition contract. Invalid requests throw before publication; a live
153:  * run is holder-owned, its result never rejects, cancellation and disposal are
154:  * bounded, and disposal waits for child cleanup within that bound. Lifecycle
155:  * listener failures are contained, and `workflow/end` fires exactly once as the
156:  * result settles.
157:  */
158: export abstract class WorkflowEngine extends Service {
159:   constructor(ctx: Context) {
160:     super(ctx, 'workflowEngine')
161:   }
162: 
163:   /**
164:    * Parse and execute a workflow script.
165:    * @param request - the script, its `args`, the parent agent, and an
166:    *   optional cancel signal.
167:    * @returns the live run; its `result` resolves when the script settles.
168:    */
169:   abstract start(request: WorkflowStartRequest): WorkflowRun
170: 
171:   /**
172:    * Emit a lifecycle event while containing and logging each listener failure.
173:    * @param name - the `workflow/*` event to dispatch.
174:    * @param args - the event's payload, matching its declared signature.
175:    */
176:   protected emitWorkflowEvent(name: WorkflowEventName, ...args: unknown[]): void {
177:     for (const callback of this.ctx.events.dispatch('emit', [name, ...args])) {
178:       try {
179:         const returned: unknown = (callback as (...payload: unknown[]) => unknown)(...args)
180:         void Promise.resolve(returned).catch((error: unknown) => {
181:           this.ctx.logger.warn(`workflow: ${name} listener rejected: ${renderListenerError(error)}`)
182:         })
183:       } catch (error: unknown) {
184:         this.ctx.logger.warn(`workflow: ${name} listener threw: ${renderListenerError(error)}`)
185:       }
186:     }
187:   }
188: }
189: 
190: /**
191:  * Render any thrown value without violating listener containment.
192:  * @param error - any thrown value.
193:  * @returns `String(error)`, or a fixed label when even coercion throws.
194:  */
195: function renderListenerError(error: unknown): string {
196:   try {
197:     return String(error)
198:   } catch {
199:     // String coercion itself may throw.
200:     return '[unrenderable thrown value]'
201:   }
202: }
203: 
204: export default WorkflowEngine

1: # @deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-workflow
2: 
3: English | [中文](README.zh.md)
4: 
5: The model-facing **`workflow` tool**: run a JavaScript orchestration script that fans out subagents, and return the script's final value. This package owns the model-facing schema and run lifecycle over [`ctx.workflowEngine`](../workflow/README.md); script parsing, execution, caps, and cancellation live behind the seam, while the consumer retains ownership of the parent-facing schema and result envelope.
6: 
7: ## What the model sees
8: 
9: Three parameters: `meta` (required identity data: `name`, `description`, and optional progress annotations), `script` (required plain JavaScript body — no `export const meta` statement; the tool description carries the complete authoring contract), and `args` (optional JSON object exposed to the script as the `args` global; wrap a bare list in a field so the wire schema stays honest). The plugin also contributes a `tool:<toolName>` system-prompt section carrying the usage policy — use the tool only on an explicit user ask for a workflow / large orchestration; prefer plain subagent calls for one or two delegations — per the convention that tool guidance ships with the tool plugin, never in the deployment persona.
10: 
11: ## Lifecycle
12: 
13: Collection is synchronous (like [`dsh-tool-subagent`](../../subagent/tool-subagent/README.md)): `execute` starts a run and awaits `run.result` inside a `try/finally` that always disposes the run, so the script and its children reach quiescence on every path. `exec.signal` is bridged to `run.cancel()` (including the already-aborted-before-start case). A non-`completed` stop reason maps to an `isError` result reporting the reason—never partial output as success; a parse/meta failure thrown synchronously by `start()` becomes an `isError` the model can correct from. Completion returns canonical `{ runId, agentsStarted, result }`; the Native renderer preserves the meta name, agent count, and JSON value, truncating only that projection at `maxResultChars`.
14: 
15: For a root transport execution (`exec.parent` absent), the tool also projects the run into the calling Agent's Session: run-start after `start()` returns, matching member starts and endings filtered by `run.id`, then run-end only after `run.result` is available and `dispose()` has reached quiescence. Nested transport calls execute normally but write no workflow record. The first failed Session append disables later recording for that run, emits one warning, and leaves either no record or a legal continuous prefix without changing the tool result or cleanup.
16: 
17: The browser-safe `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-workflow/types` subpath owns these four log-only event payloads and their `SessionEventMap` declaration. The package invariant rejects duplicate starts, unpaired members, terminal events with open members, and updates after run-end on both cold load and live append while accepting missing terminal suffixes.
18: 
19: ## Render intent
20: 
21: Decided up front (per the [render-intent Agent Note](../../../.agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-07-02-tool-render-intent-union.md)): a `generic` card titled `workflow: <meta.name>`, read directly from `args.meta.name` (presentation is a pure function of args and does not ask the engine to parse); the script text rides as `rawInput`. The result keeps the generic card.
22: 
23: ## Config
24: 
25: | Key | Default | Meaning |
26: |---|---|---|
27: | `toolName` | `workflow` | The model-facing tool name to register. |
28: | `maxResultChars` | `50000` | Rendered-result ceiling; longer JSON is truncated with a notice. |
29: 
30: ## Model Experience
31: 
32: ### System prompt
33: 
34: #### What the model sees
35: 
36: Every parent request in this plugin's registration scope receives the workflow guidance below. A scoped tool restriction can hide the schema without removing this independently registered guidance.
37: 
38: ##### Workflow guidance
39: 
40: ```markdown
41: Use the <toolName> tool ONLY when the user explicitly asks for a workflow or for large multi-agent orchestration: you write a JavaScript script (the tool description documents the exact format) that fans work out across many subagents with phases and structured results. For one or two delegations, prefer plain subagent calls.
42: ```
43: 
44: #### Token effect
45: 
46: Small fixed guidance cost per request while the plugin is active.
47: 
48: #### KV Cache effect
49: 
50: Prefix-stable while the plugin scope and guidance text are unchanged. Activation or disposal may invalidate reuse from this prompt section.
51: 
52: ### Tool schema
53: 
54: #### What the model sees
55: 
56: When visible, the generated default [`workflow` schema](../../../docs/tool-catalog.md#deepseek-aidsh-tool-workflow) carries the complete JavaScript hook and metadata contract; `toolName` can rename the definition, and the model submits script, metadata, and optional args.
57: 
58: #### Token effect
59: 
60: Substantial fixed schema cost on each request where the tool is visible.
61: 
62: #### KV Cache effect
63: 
64: Prefix-stable while `toolName`, definition, and visibility are unchanged. Renaming, plugin lifecycle, or scoped restrictions may invalidate reuse from this schema.
65: 
66: ### Tool-call history and result
67: 
68: #### What the model sees
69: 
70: The full model-written script, metadata, and args remain in the assistant tool call. Success is exactly `workflow "<name>" completed (<count> agent<optional-s>).`, newline, `Return value:`, newline, and pretty-printed data-dependent JSON; a cap adds `… [truncated: <omitted> more characters]` on a new line. Failures are exactly `Error: workflow run was cancelled`, optionally suffixed ` (<error>)`, `Error: workflow run failed: <error-or-unknown error>`, or defensively `Error: workflow run ended abnormally (<reason>)`; a call without an owning agent becomes `Error: workflow tool requires a calling agent (exec.agent was undefined)`. Intermediate child messages are omitted.
71: 
72: #### Token effect
73: 
74: Call tokens can be large and remain until compaction. Result rendering is capped by `maxResultChars`; child-model tokens are separate from the parent's retained context.
75: 
76: #### KV Cache effect
77: 
78: Append-only; newly visible content follows the reusable request prefix and does not invalidate existing KV-cache entries.
79: 
80: ## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
81: 
82: - **The parent turn blocks until the whole workflow settles** — there is no background start/poll API, and cancellation discards partial output as an error.
83: - **`args` must be an object and Native result text is bounded** — callers wrap top-level arrays/scalars in a field; the canonical workflow result remains complete, while JSON beyond `maxResultChars` is truncated in the model-facing projection rather than stored behind a retrieval handle.
84: - **Workflow policy is fixed per tool registration** — provider selection, caps, and tool name are deployment config, not model-call arguments.
85: - **Durable records are top-level and observational** — nested Code Mode dispatches are not recorded, and a recording failure intentionally degrades to an incomplete prefix rather than changing execution.

(End of file - total 85 lines)
</content>
